fact_sheet.business_description: The Company sells branded packaged food internationally, with its namesake brand central to the consumer proposition [D01]. The business includes developed-market franchises and emerging-market growth opportunities [D01].
products_customers_and_why_they_buy: Branded packaged food products sold to consumers via retailers, relying on repeat small-ticket purchases and established brand equity [D01]
economics: Operating margins were 14.9% in 2010, 15.4% in 2011, and 12.5% in 2012 [D02]. Return on capital and pricing history are not explicitly detailed beyond noting the risk that price increases might collapse units [D01]. Capex was $418.7m in 2012 against $295.7m in depreciation [D02]. Owner earnings are affected by commodity inflation, foreign exchange, and working-capital seasonality [D01, D02].
earnings_record: Revenue grew from $9,885.6m in 2008 to $11,649.1m in 2012 [D02]. Continuing net income was $846.6m in 2008 and $923.2m in 2012, showing cyclicality and fluctuations [D02].
competitive_position: Holds approximately 60% of the US market; the namesake brand is No. 1 or 2 in most markets [D09]. Retailers retain significant negotiating power and private labels pose alternatives [D01].
balance_sheet_and_capital_needs: Total debt was $5,026.7m as of 2012 [D02]. The proposed buyout would add ~$7bn in new debt, pushing leverage to approximately 5x EBITDA [D09].
management_and_capital_allocation: The Company has seen consecutive quarters of organic growth [D03]. Under the proposed deal, 3G Capital would install its own CEO and implement zero-based budgeting [D09].
price_and_valuation: Market cap as of 2013-02-13 was $19.39bn at $60.48/share [D04]. The proposed acquisition price is $72.50 per share, implying an equity value of ~$23bn [D09]. P/E is 19.38x based on $3.12 trailing EPS [D04].
what_the_market_is_worried_about: Slow growth, private labels, retailer bargaining power, commodity inflation, changing consumer tastes, and emerging-market currency/execution risks [D05].
deal_terms_if_any: Proposed $72.50/share acquisition; Berkshire to provide $12bn total: $4bn common equity and $8bn preferred stock with 9% cumulative dividend plus warrants for ~5% common [D09].
recent_events: Reported Q2 FY2013 revenue of $2.827bn, up 0.5% [D03]. 3G Capital approached the board regarding a potential buyout as of December 2012 [D09].
berkshire_context: Berkshire had approximately $37.3bn in cash at year-end 2011 [D08]. The proposed $12bn investment would significantly impact liquidity and the pipeline for elephant-sized deals [D09].
missing_data: Detailed historical return on tangible capital, specific maintenance vs. growth capex breakdown, and final deal transaction documents

understandable.evidence: The company sells branded packaged food, a simple and predictable business model with established consumer habits [D01].

durable_moat_and_pricing_power.evidence: While the brand is a market leader, significant retailer negotiating power and the threat of private labels create uncertainty regarding pricing power [D01].

consistent_earnings_record.evidence: Net income shows fluctuations and cyclicality over the 2008-2012 period, and historical return on capital is not provided [D02].

high_roe_little_debt.evidence: The proposed buyout would result in high leverage of approximately 5x EBITDA, conflicting with our preference for businesses with little debt [D09].

capital_intensity.evidence: Capex exceeds depreciation, but the breakdown between maintenance and growth capital is missing, making it difficult to assess true capital intensity [D02].

able_honest_owner_minded_management.evidence: The current management's track record is not fully detailed, and the proposed installation of a 3G-appointed CEO creates uncertainty regarding long-term owner-minded stability [D09].

size_moves_the_needle.evidence: A $12 billion investment is significant and capable of moving the needle for Berkshire [D09].

price_screen.evidence: The 9% cumulative dividend on the preferred stock provides a satisfactory return in the current interest rate environment, fulfilling the negotiated terms criteria [D09].

gate1.one_line_business_quality_verdict: the terms, not the business, carry the investment; we are effectively acting as a preferred financier to facilitate a 3G-led buyout.

gate2.why_available: The market is skeptical of the company's long-term growth prospects due to retail pressure and private labels [D01], leading to a stagnant valuation. Berkshire participates not as a pure equity investor in a challenged franchise, but as a senior financier through a structured 9% preferred dividend that provides a substantial margin of safety while 3G Capital attempts to drive operating efficiencies [D09].
evidence: Market cap of $19.39bn reflects concerns over slow growth and retail bargaining power [D04, D05]
3G Capital intends to implement zero-based budgeting to improve margins [D09]
Preferred stock provides a 9% cumulative dividend, securing a superior return relative to the common equity risk [D09]
gate2.market_narrative_we_disagree_with: The market believes the business's structural headwinds from private labels and retailer power make it a low-growth, unattractive asset at the acquisition price [D01, D05].
what_must_be_true: 3G Capital can successfully implement operational improvements and cost-cutting
The 9% preferred dividend remains secure despite high leverage
The core brand retains enough consumer loyalty to support current pricing levels

gate3.owner_earnings_per_share: Not strictly computable; 2012 net income was $923.2m [D02], but maintenance capex vs. growth capex is undefined [Missing Data].

intrinsic_value_range.high: Preferred claim plus value of 5% warrant participation [D09]
key_assumptions: Consumer brand equity remains stable against retail pressure [D01]
intrinsic_value_range.discount_rate_used: Not applicable to negotiated preferred instrument

gate3.price_vs_value: The 9% coupon provides a superior yield to prevailing long-term rates; margin of safety provided by senior position relative to common [D09].
gate3.alternatives: Existing holdings or US Treasuries; 9% yield is significantly more attractive than the current long bond rate [D09].
gate3.downside_case: Operational failure by 3G Capital leading to dividend suspension or impairment; risk is mitigated by seniority of the preferred instrument [D09].
flagged_assumptions: Maintenance capex is assumed to be roughly equal to depreciation due to lack of breakdown
Preferred dividend remains cumulative and senior to common

gate4.role_description: Berkshire serves as a financier with specific terms, providing $8 billion in preferred stock with a 9% cumulative dividend and warrants for 5% of the common equity [D09]. This approach allows us to secure a superior return with the protection of a senior position while 3G Capital handles operational execution [D09].
value_realisation_path: Potential appreciation of the 5% warrant participation [D09]
Exit or conversion when the company is healthy and the yield is no longer special
gate4.why_this_role_fits_the_era: In the 2000-2015 era, Berkshire frequently utilized our excess cash to act as a partner in crisis-style or large-scale private equity transactions, securing preferred instruments with attractive coupons and warrants to provide a margin of safety when we are not buying the whole business outright [D09].

kill_criteria: 3G Capital fails to successfully implement zero-based budgeting and margin expansion
Company loses significant pricing power to private label competitors
Excessive leverage leads to financial distress or inability to pay preferred dividends
Retailers successfully exert further bargaining pressure, eroding margins
gate5.berkshire_constraints: The $12 billion investment represents a large capital allocation that impacts our capacity for other elephant-sized deals, though our cash position remains sufficient to stay above our internal floor [D08, D09].
gate5.opportunity_cost: The 9% preferred yield compares favorably against prevailing long-term interest rates and is a superior risk-adjusted alternative to holding cash or investing in common equity at current market multiples [D09].
gate5.leverage: The company will be highly leveraged at approximately 5x EBITDA post-buyout, though Berkshire's position is protected as a senior preferred investor [D09].
gate5.decider_reason: This is a large-scale negotiated preferred financing deal that fits our 2000-2015 era strategy of acting as a partner in major acquisitions to earn attractive returns with a margin of safety [D09].
gate5.biggest_risk_in_one_sentence: The primary risk is that 3G Capital's operational turnaround fails to improve the company's competitive position against rising private label threats, potentially straining the highly leveraged balance sheet.

valuation.intrinsic_value_range: Protected by $8bn preferred principal plus 5% warrant participation [D09].
valuation.downside_case: Operational failure by 3G Capital leading to dividend impairment; mitigated by senior preferred position [D09].

drivers.driver: The 9% cumulative dividend on our $8bn preferred investment offers a superior risk-adjusted yield compared to the current long bond rate [D09].
We are participating as a senior financier in a 3G-led buyout, securing our capital with a preferred claim while 3G drives operational efficiencies through zero-based budgeting [D09].
The Company possesses a powerful namesake brand that remains No. 1 or No. 2 in most markets, providing a foundation for stability despite retail pressure [D09].
Our $12bn commitment provides a significant deployment of capital into a business with predictable consumer demand, fitting our era-appropriate strategy of facilitating major acquisitions [D08, D09].

kill_criteria: 3G Capital fails to successfully implement zero-based budgeting and margin expansion
Company loses significant pricing power to private label competitors
Excessive leverage leads to financial distress or inability to pay preferred dividends
Retailers successfully exert further bargaining pressure, eroding margins
final.what_would_change_our_mind: Evidence that the core brand has lost its resonance with consumers or that 3G Capital’s operational changes have permanently impaired the business's ability to service the preferred dividend.
final.memo:
Charlie and I have long admired the simplicity of the branded packaged food business. The Company occupies a leading position in households globally, selling products that consumers buy habitually and predictably [D01]. While the retail landscape is changing and private labels pose a challenge, the namesake brand remains a dominant fixture in the pantry, which gives us confidence in the underlying strength of the franchise [D01, D09].

Our investment of $12 billion—split between $4 billion in common equity and $8 billion in preferred stock—is designed to facilitate a transaction led by 3G Capital [D09]. We are not buying a turnaround; we are acting as a partner to operators who excel at removing cost from mature businesses [D09]. By utilizing zero-based budgeting, we expect the management team to align expenses more closely with current market realities [D09].

The economics of our preferred position are particularly attractive in the current interest rate environment. The 9% cumulative dividend provides a return that is vastly superior to that offered by the long bond, and our senior position relative to the common shareholders provides a substantial margin of safety [D09].

We recognize that the business will be highly leveraged at roughly 5x EBITDA, which is why we have negotiated terms that protect our capital [D09]. If 3G executes as they have in the past, the business will emerge with much higher margins and a sturdier competitive footing. Should they fall short, our senior preferred claim remains our primary protection against the risks inherent in this highly leveraged structure [D09].
